tweets.text: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

One of the least explored questions in AI is how to build rich open-ended environments for learning. Benchmarks evaluate intelligence, environments shape it. iLands is interesting because it doesn't just measure agents by how much money they make, it forces them to survive in a living market. “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). Yes, open-source / open-weight models are important for a healthy AI ecosystem. That's how we can verify things, check claims, and keep up outside the closed labs. Plus, it gives us the freedom to run AI on our own hardware if we are not ready to share personal data and IPs with closed labs through using their models. (Not that proprietary models are bad, actually I use them a lot as well, but it wouldn't healthy not to have any alternatives.) Anyway, while pretty much everyone is waiting for the Kimi K3 and Ling 3.0 weights to land on the model hub any day now, there were quite a few other interesting new open-weight model releases the past week. Yes, one of those weeks! So, here are the architecture pics along with some notes on what I found most interesting: 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B uses looped depth sharing. This basically means it runs the same 22-layer (=transformer block) stack twice. So, it extends the 22-layer architecture to 44-layers, but without duplicating the weights. (2x the transformer block compute but same memory footprint.) Why? The info is a bit sparse, but section 2.1 of the Nanbeige 4.2 technical report says two passes gave the best trade-off and retained about 75% of the token efficiency of a standard architecture. More passes gave barely any gains but made the training much slower and much more expensive. 2) Laguna S 2.1 is poolside's Laguna model in a really nice size: 118B sparse MoE with 8B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. Otherwise, the architecture is pretty standard. It uses 36 sliding-window and 12 global (gated-)GQA layers. However, given this size, and the fact that it (just barely) runs on my DGX Spark (uses about <80 GB of RAM), this is right now the most interesting model for me personally. It's 3x bigger and thus a tad slower but maybe a good candidate as daily-driver-Qwen3.6-35B-replacement. (Still waiting on some more independent performance benchmarks though.) 3) Motif-3-Beta is a new 314B-A13B sparse MoE that is somewhat based on DeepSeek V4 in terms of mHC and latent attention. But it uses a new component, Grouped Differential Latent Attention, which is inspired by Multi-head Latent Attention. I probably should write an article about this some time, but for now, the tl;dr is as follows. Regular MLA compresses the keys and values into a smaller latent representation to mainly reduce the KV cache size. GDLA does a similar low-rank compression but puts the attention heads into groups and also learns a noise head for each group where the noise gets subtracted for filtering purposes... Anyway, a topic for another day! 4) Solar Open 2 is a new 250B-A15B hybrid MoE by Upstage that interleaves three Kimi Delta Attention layers with one GQA layer. 5) Antares 1B is a small model (and there is also an even smaller 0.3B variant) from Cisco starts that with the IBM Granite 4.0 1B backbone and uses SFT plus GRPO for terminal-based cybersecurity stuff. It is a nice example of task-specific post-training on a genuinely small model. 6) BTL-3 is a rank-32 LoRA adapter for Qwen3.6-27B aimed at coding agents and structured tool use. The really strong benchmark performance suggests that LoRA adapters are still a useful tool/technique in 2026. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

Here's the closing message I sent to everyone today. My dear friends! Today’s my last day at OpenAI. I have been thinking a lot about what I wanted to say in my final remarks to the company. Here are a few things I hope everyone takes deeply to heart. 1. For All of Humanity. What we have been building here is an opportunity to improve the human condition unlike any other in history. It’s easy to get distracted by the wealth and power that comes with this. It’s easy to focus on the already wealthy and powerful in the world, because they demand so much of our attention as customers or lawmakers or competitors. Nonetheless, do not lose sight of the “all” in “all of humanity.” Our mission for everyone. Working people. People in poverty. People who dream of a better life. What we are building can help them. It is our mission to ensure that it does. To that end, yesterday I donated a major gift to GiveDirectly, a charity that makes direct cash transfers to people in poverty in Africa and in the United States. This is a highly effective way of helping people; I encourage others to consider giving as well. 2. Risk Is Our Business. Technology changes the security equilibrium of the world profoundly and creates new risks. Some of these risks will directly result from AI; many others will result from other fields of science and engineering that are accelerated by AI. Risk is inextricable from progress. It is not a reason to turn our back on progress. I think, from time to time, of a speech from Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek—“Risk is our business,” he says about humanity as a whole. I believe this is true. But we should also be cognizant of the risks and we should actively manage them. We can simultaneously believe that it will require extraordinary effort to accomplish the safety and security of humanity, while committing to making that effort in support of our work to advance the technological frontier. The question of progress and safety is not either/or. It is definitively “both.” 3. The Consent of the Governed. OpenAI, and especially the OpenAI Foundation, will be among the most important organizations in the world. The level of power concentrated here will be like the power of a state. It demands a level of accountability that exceeds that of an ordinary company. I encourage OpenAI to pursue a path of governance innovation that makes it progressively more democratic and more beholden to the consent of the governed. All of humanity will be impacted by the work here; all of humanity should have some way to weigh in eventually. There is no roadmap for what form this should take. This is an ideal. But I hold it entirely. Thank you all again so much for being a part of an unbelievable nine year journey with me. To Safe AGI!

Download finishes -> you start training. 2. Fresh crawl. v2 was a 2023 snapshot of even older crawls. v3 is a direct re-crawl of GitHub at the latest commit, completed by August 2025: 224M repositories, 44B files. Forks were only included if they had 5+ stars. Two ways in: 🥞 stack-v3-train - near-deduplicated, quality-filtered, PII-redacted, contents inline. Roll your own dedup, filters, and mixes. huggingface.co/buckets/Huggi… The record isn't really ours to claim - it's millions of everyone's repositories, neatly stacked. processed.summary: Cette semaine, le monde de l'IA a été effervescent, avec des avancées marquantes sur plusieurs fronts. Les modèles d'IA comme GPT-5.6 Sol et Claude Opus 5 démontrent des capacités impressionnantes à résoudre des problèmes complexes en mathématiques et à transformer la productivité personnelle et professionnelle, notamment via des interfaces vocales et des agents autonomes. Un débat important se poursuit sur l'équilibre entre les modèles d'IA 'ouverts' (dont le code est partagé) et 'fermés' (propriétaires), avec des arguments pour la sécurité et l'innovation, tandis que de nouveaux outils et modèles continuent d'émerger, rendant l'IA toujours plus accessible et polyvalente.

glossaire.definition: Un modèle d'intelligence artificielle dont le 'cerveau' (les poids) est rendu public, permettant à quiconque de l'étudier, de l'améliorer et de l'utiliser.
Un modèle d'intelligence artificielle dont le fonctionnement interne et les données d'entraînement sont gardés secrets par l'entreprise qui l'a créé.
Un modèle linguistique de grande taille capable de comprendre et de générer du texte de manière très fluide et cohérente.
Un système d'IA capable d'effectuer des tâches complexes de manière autonome, en planifiant, en exécutant des actions et en s'adaptant à son environnement.
Le processus par lequel un modèle d'IA utilise ce qu'il a appris pour faire des prédictions ou générer des réponses à de nouvelles données.
Une architecture de modèle où différentes parties du modèle (les 'experts') se spécialisent dans le traitement de types de données spécifiques, le tout étant coordonné par un 'réseau de portail'.
L'art de concevoir des instructions (prompts) efficaces pour guider un modèle d'IA afin qu'il produise les résultats souhaités.

highlights.text_fr: «Oui, les modèles open-source / open-weight sont importants pour un écosystème d'IA sain. C'est ainsi que nous pouvons vérifier les choses, contrôler les affirmations et nous tenir au courant en dehors des laboratoires fermés. De plus, cela nous donne la liberté de faire fonctionner l'IA sur notre propre matériel si nous ne sommes pas prêts à partager des données personnelles et des IPs avec des laboratoires fermés en utilisant leurs modèles. (Non pas que les modèles propriétaires soient mauvais, en fait je les utilise aussi beaucoup, mais il ne serait pas sain de ne pas avoir d'alternatives.) Quoi qu'il en soit, alors que presque tout le monde attend que les poids de Kimi K3 et Ling 3.0 arrivent sur le hub de modèles d'un jour à l'autre, il y a eu pas mal d'autres nouvelles sorties de modèles open-weight intéressantes la semaine dernière. Oui, une de ces semaines ! Alors, voici les images d'architecture ainsi que quelques notes sur ce que j'ai trouvé le plus intéressant : 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B utilise le partage de profondeur en boucle. Cela signifie qu'il exécute deux fois la même pile de 22 couches (= bloc de transformateur). Il étend donc l'architecture de 22 couches à 44 couches, mais sans dupliquer les poids. (2x la puissance de calcul du bloc de transformateur mais la même empreinte mémoire.) Pourquoi ? Les informations sont un peu rares, mais la section 2.1 du rapport technique de Nanbeige 4.2 indique que deux passes ont donné le meilleur compromis et ont conservé environ 75% de l'efficacité des tokens d'une architecture standard. Plus de passes ont apporté peu de gains mais ont rendu l'entraînement beaucoup plus lent et beaucoup plus coûteux. 2) Laguna S 2.1 est le modèle Laguna de poolside dans une très belle taille : 118B sparse MoE avec 8B de paramètres actifs et une fenêtre de contexte de 1M de tokens. Sinon, l'architecture est assez standard. Il utilise 36 couches de fenêtre glissante et 12 couches GQA (gated-)globales. Cependant, compte tenu de cette taille, et du fait qu'il fonctionne (tout juste) sur mon DGX Spark (utilise environ <80 Go de RAM), c'est actuellement le modèle le plus intéressant pour moi personnellement. Il est 3x plus grand et donc un peu plus lent mais peut-être un bon candidat pour remplacer le Qwen3.6-35B quotidien. (J'attends encore des benchmarks de performance plus indépendants.) 3) Motif-3-Beta est un nouveau MoE sparse 314B-A13B qui est quelque peu basé sur DeepSeek V4 en termes de mHC et d'attention latente. Mais il utilise un nouveau composant, l'attention latente différentielle groupée, qui est inspirée de l'attention latente multi-têtes. Je devrais probablement écrire un article à ce sujet un jour, mais pour l'instant, le tl;dr est le suivant. Le MLA régulier compresse les clés et les valeurs dans une représentation latente plus petite pour réduire principalement la taille du cache KV. highlights.text_original: Yes, open-source / open-weight models are important for a healthy AI ecosystem. That's how we can verify things, check claims, and keep up outside the closed labs. Plus, it gives us the freedom to run AI on our own hardware if we are not ready to share personal data and IPs with closed labs through using their models. (Not that proprietary models are bad, actually I use them a lot as well, but it wouldn't healthy not to have any alternatives.) Anyway, while pretty much everyone is waiting for the Kimi K3 and Ling 3.0 weights to land on the model hub any day now, there were quite a few other interesting new open-weight model releases the past week. Yes, one of those weeks! So, here are the architecture pics along with some notes on what I found most interesting: 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B uses looped depth sharing. This basically means it runs the same 22-layer (=transformer block) stack twice. So, it extends the 22-layer architecture to 44-layers, but without duplicating the weights. (2x the transformer block compute but same memory footprint.) Why? The info is a bit sparse, but section 2.1 of the Nanbeige 4.2 technical report says two passes gave the best trade-off and retained about 75% of the token efficiency of a standard architecture. More passes gave barely any gains but made the training much slower and much more expensive. 2) Laguna S 2.1 is poolside's Laguna model in a really nice size: 118B sparse MoE with 8B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. Otherwise, the architecture is pretty standard. It uses 36 sliding-window and 12 global (gated-)GQA layers. However, given this size, and the fact that it (just barely) runs on my DGX Spark (uses about <80 GB of RAM), this is right now the most interesting model for me personally. It's 3x bigger and thus a tad slower but maybe a good candidate as daily-driver-Qwen3.6-35B-replacement. (Still waiting on some more independent performance benchmarks though.) 3) Motif-3-Beta is a new 314B-A13B sparse MoE that is somewhat based on DeepSeek V4 in terms of mHC and latent attention. But it uses a new component, Grouped Differential Latent Attention, which is inspired by Multi-head Latent Attention. I probably should write an article about this some time, but for now, the tl;dr is as follows. Regular MLA compresses the keys and values into a smaller latent representation to mainly reduce the KV cache size. GDLA does a similar low-rank compression but puts the attention heads into groups and also learns a noise head for each group where the noise gets subtracted for filtering purposes... Anyway, a topic for another day! 4) Solar Open 2 is a new 250B-A15B hybrid MoE by Upstage that interleaves three Kimi Delta Attention layers with one GQA layer. 5) Antares 1B is a small model (and there is also an even smaller 0.3B variant) from Cisco starts that with the IBM Granite 4.0 1B backbone and uses SFT plus GRPO for terminal-based cybersecurity stuff. It is a nice example of task-specific post-training on a genuinely small model. 6) BTL-3 is a rank-32 LoRA adapter for Qwen3.6-27B aimed at coding agents and structured tool use. The really strong benchmark performance suggests that LoRA adapters are still a useful tool/technique in 2026. I added all six to the LLM Architecture Gallery for some additional details: sebastianraschka.com/llm-arc…

tips.text_fr: «Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne longue session de radotage. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste radoter pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, n'importe quoi, un flux de conscience complet. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont en quelque sorte très bons pour reconstruire de longs radotages incohérents et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort un peu plus propre que ce que vous aviez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la "fusion mentale" et avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.»
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

tips.text_fr: «"L'ingénierie de boucles" est un mot à la mode après que des mentions de Boris Cherny (le créateur de Claude Code) et Peter Steinberger (le créateur d'OpenClaw) soient devenues virales sur les réseaux sociaux. Les boucles sont désormais un élément clé de la façon dont nous faisons itérer les agents IA longuement pour construire des logiciels. Dans cette lettre, j'aimerais partager mes 3 boucles clés, présentées dans l'image ci-dessous, pour construire des produits 0-à-1. Ces boucles guident non seulement la façon dont je construis des logiciels, mais aussi la façon dont je décide quel logiciel construire. Boucle de codage agentique : Étant donné une spécification produit et éventuellement un ensemble d'évaluations (c'est-à-dire un ensemble de données pour mesurer les performances), nous pouvons demander à un agent IA d'écrire du code, de tester son travail et de continuer à itérer jusqu'à ce que le code soit exempt de bugs et conforme à sa spécification. Cette idée de boucler a pris son envol vers la fin de l'année dernière, et elle a changé la donne en permettant aux agents de codage de travailler plus longtemps de manière productive sans intervention humaine. Par exemple, ce week-end, je construisais une application pour ma fille pour qu'elle s'exerce à taper, et mon agent de codage pouvait facilement travailler pendant environ une heure, utilisant un navigateur web pour vérifier ce qu'il avait construit plusieurs fois avant de me revenir, sans nécessiter mon intervention. La boucle d'ingénierie s'exécute rapidement. Toutes les quelques minutes, l'agent de codage pourrait construire et tester une nouvelle version du logiciel. J'entends fréquemment des développeurs qui trouvent de nouvelles façons d'ingénierie des boucles d'ingénierie plus efficaces. C'est un domaine d'invention actif ! Boucle de rétroaction du développeur : Dans cette boucle, un développeur examine le produit actuel et dirige l'agent de codage pour l'améliorer. L'année dernière, de nombreux développeurs (y compris moi) agissaient comme la fonction QA (assurance qualité) pour nos agents de codage, trouvant manuellement les bugs et demandant ensuite à l'agent de les corriger. Mais avec les agents de codage beaucoup plus capables de tester leur propre code, le temps que nous devons consacrer à cette fonction a considérablement diminué. Cela nous permet de prendre des décisions produit de niveau supérieur, comme les fonctionnalités clés à offrir, là où l'interface utilisateur a besoin d'être améliorée, etc. La boucle de rétroaction du développeur opère sur des intervalles de temps allant de dizaines de minutes à des heures — c'est la fréquence à laquelle un développeur pourrait examiner un produit et donner son avis. Dans le cas de l'application de dactylographie, j'ai changé d'avis plusieurs fois sur la conception visuelle, quels costumes de chat elle peut débloquer à mesure qu'elle apprend (elle adore les chats), et le flux utilisateur pour qu'un adulte puisse se connecter et diriger l'expérience d'apprentissage de l'enfant. Lorsqu'un développeur a une vision claire de ce qu'il veut construire, c'est encore beaucoup de travail de traduire cette vision en une spécification pour qu'un agent de codage l'implémente. De plus, après que le développeur a vu une implémentation, il pourrait mettre à jour (ou peut-être clarifier) la spécification pour l'orienter vers ce qu'il veut. Si vous constatez que le système rencontre à plusieurs reprises certains problèmes, la construction d'un ensemble d'évaluations pour l'agent devient utile. Les équipes nativement IA utilisent de plus en plus l'IA pour aider à façonner la direction du produit, par exemple, en automatisant la collecte et l'analyse des données d'utilisation, en résumant les retours clients écrits et verbaux, ou en effectuant une analyse concurrentielle. Cependant, pour à peu près tous les produits dans lesquels je suis impliqué, je constate que les humains ont un avantage contextuel significatif sur les systèmes d'IA actuels — nous en savons beaucoup plus que le système d'IA sur les utilisateurs et le contexte dans lequel le produit doit fonctionner — et les humains jouent donc un rôle critique. Beaucoup de gens décrivent cette contribution humaine comme du "goût", mais je préfère la considérer comme un avantage contextuel des humains, car cela nous donne une voie plus claire pour aider les systèmes d'IA à s'améliorer. Cela explique également pourquoi cette étape ne peut pas être automatisée : tant que l'humain sait quelque chose que l'IA ignore, l'humain dans la boucle est nécessaire pour injecter cette connaissance dans le système. Boucle de rétroaction externe : Cela inclut un large éventail de tactiques comme demander l'avis de quelques amis, lancer des tests alpha, ou mettre le code en production avec des tests A/B. Ces tactiques sont généralement lentes, prenant rarement moins de quelques heures et parfois des jours, voire des semaines. Ces données informent la vision du développeur, qui à son tour continue de piloter la spécification détaillée du produit, qui à son tour pilote l'agent de codage. Avec les agents de codage accélérant le développement logiciel, de plus en plus d'ingénieurs commencent à jouer un rôle partiel de gestion de produit. Pour de nombreux ingénieurs qui évoluent vers ce rôle, la partie la plus difficile est de façonner la vision du produit et de trouver un équilibre entre la construction (combler le fossé entre la vision et la spécification) et l'obtention des retours utilisateurs pour faire évoluer la vision. Il est important de faire les deux ! J'écrirai davantage sur la façon de faire cela dans de futurs articles, mais pour l'instant, je trouve encourageant que les ingénieurs jouent un rôle élargi (tout comme les chefs de produit et les designers font désormais plus d'ingénierie). [Texte original : The Batch]»
tips.text_original: “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). [Original text: The Batch]

idees.text_fr: «Adam Thierer a écrit le livre fondateur sur l'"Innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas à demander l'autorisation au gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. Protéger l'IA open source est maintenant un élément essentiel pour garantir cela. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) Nous sommes à un carrefour critique dans le débat sur la gouvernance de l'IA aux États-Unis, et il semble que nous nous rapprochions d'une bataille très sérieuse sur la question de savoir si les modèles open source seront même autorisés dans un environnement où un nouveau régime de licence de facto prend forme. En l'absence de cadres statutaires formels du Congrès ou de règles administratives claires (comme la révision de la règle de diffusion), il semble que nous soyons confrontés à un processus sporadiques, arbitraire et non transparent d'examen des modèles. La fiction des accords "volontaires" plane sur ce débat, et certains grands développeurs de modèles montrent déjà une incroyable volonté de faire des pieds et des mains pour satisfaire les responsables / ordres liés à la sécurité nationale auxquels le reste d'entre nous n'avons pas accès. C'est un processus très opaque. Et ces développeurs de modèles sont censés collaborer avec ces fonctionnaires, sinon leurs modèles seront retirés du marché ou bloqués pendant de longues périodes. Ou ils perdront tous les contrats d'approvisionnement gouvernementaux qu'ils ont. Il n'y a rien de "volontaire" quand cette épée de Damoclès plane dans la pièce. Alors que ce désordre s'aggrave, à un moment donné, la question de la gestion des modèles open source sera mise en lumière plus clairement car elle devra l'être. J'ai même entendu des rumeurs dernièrement selon lesquelles quelque chose pourrait venir de l'administration sur ce front pour y remédier. Inutile de dire que si ce nouveau régime informel d'examen des modèles d'IA s'étend et prend davantage de caractéristiques / d'exigences de pré-validation, il est difficile de voir comment les acteurs open source pourraient se conformer à une telle quasi-licence des modèles d'IA. Plus précisément, si ce nouveau régime ambigu s'accompagne d'une présomption générale de "restreindre jusqu'à ce que permis", alors cela signifierait la fin de l'open source. C'est une voie très sombre pour notre pays. Pire encore, bien sûr, serait une décision des responsables de la sécurité nationale de restreindre plus directement les modèles et les capacités open source. Si cela se produit, alors nous serions de retour au cœur d'une bataille de type "Clipper Chip" comme ce que nous avons vu à la fin des années 1990. C'est une voie beaucoup plus sombre pour l'Amérique. Pendant ce temps, les développeurs open source n'ont pas d'"actions d'or" ou d'autres avantages à offrir au gouvernement pour résoudre leurs problèmes. Soyons clairs : Si notre gouvernement prend le chemin obscur, ce sera la bataille la plus importante pour la liberté computationnelle des temps modernes. Il est temps que les gens prennent position en défense de l'open source avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m»
idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

idees.text_fr: «2023 : les LLM ont du mal avec les problèmes de mots de 4e année. 2024 : les LLM peuvent faire des maths de lycée. 2025 : les LLM obtiennent une médaille d'or aux OIM. Maintenant, GPT-5.6 résout de célèbres questions de mathématiques/statistiques de pointe. Les OIM, c'est aujourd'hui et GPT-5.6 obtenant un score parfait en 'one-shot' n'est même plus une nouvelle. Où serons-nous l'année prochaine ? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) L'IA a aidé à résoudre une question importante en statistiques. Dans le domaine des tests d'hypothèses multiples, l'objectif de contrôler le taux de fausse découverte (FDR) a été introduit dans un article fondateur par Benjamini et Hochberg (1995). Ils ont également introduit une méthode (la méthode Benjamini-Hochberg ou BH) et ont prouvé qu'elle contrôlait le FDR. Cette méthode a été largement adoptée dans la science à haut débit moderne, y compris en génomique, astronomie, économie, etc. L'article a recueilli plus de 130 000 citations à ce jour. Cependant, Benjamini et Hochberg ont montré le contrôle du FDR uniquement lorsque les données des tests individuels sont *indépendantes*. En pratique, ces données sont souvent dépendantes ; un bon exemple est les données sur les variants génétiques dus au déséquilibre de liaison. Des travaux ultérieurs se sont concentrés sur l'extension de la validité de la procédure BH, par exemple, à une forme de dépendance positive par Benjamini et Yekutieli (2001). La question de savoir quand la procédure BH contrôle le FDR est restée ouverte. Au cours des vingt dernières années, de nombreux auteurs, dont Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim et van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar et Zhang (2025), ont conjecturé que la procédure BH contrôlait le FDR pour les tests bilatéraux utilisant toutes les données gaussiennes corrélées. Ces auteurs ont présenté des preuves théoriques et empiriques étayant, mais ne montrant pas directement, la conjecture. Avec l'aide de l'IA (spécifiquement GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), j'ai tranché la question par la négative : La procédure Benjamini-Hochberg ne contrôle *pas* généralement le taux de fausse découverte au niveau souhaité pour les tests gaussiens bilatéraux corrélés. Cela a été fait en présentant un modèle factoriel gaussien pour lequel, à un niveau nominal alpha=0.01, le taux de fausse découverte est prouvé être FDR>0.0104. Il y a beaucoup de commentaires intéressants à faire : 1. Ce résultat devrait intéresser tout le monde dans le domaine des statistiques. Emmanuel Candes de l'Université de Stanford a un jour qualifié le taux de fausse découverte et la procédure Benjamini-Hochberg de "l'un des deux développements les plus importants en statistiques après 1950" (l'autre étant la régression de James-Stein). La présente conjecture est probablement la question la plus centrale concernant le FDR/BH qui était restée sans solution jusqu'à présent. 2. GPT-5.6 a résolu le problème en une seule fois après 90 minutes de raisonnement, alors qu'avec 5.5, je n'avais pas réussi à le résoudre même après avoir itéré avec plusieurs agents parallèles pendant peut-être 20 heures. L'amélioration des capacités est donc bien réelle. Des temps passionnants à vivre ! 3. L'argument n'est pas particulièrement surprenant, mais il combine une approche asymptotique (standard pour l'analyse FDR, voir par exemple Genovese et Wasserman, Efron, etc.) avec un certificat numérique d'une manière qui serait assez non standard dans le domaine. Une fois que nous avons l'exemple spécifique, des simulations simples confirment également que le taux de fausse découverte est en effet plus élevé que la valeur nominale (voir figure jointe). 4. Le degré actuel de violation par rapport au niveau nominal est relativement faible (0.104 contre 0.1). L'importance de ce résultat est donc principalement conceptuelle. Les implications pratiques restent à déterminer. Globalement, un développement passionnant ! Le prépublication est disponible ici ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) et sera sur arxiv ce soir ; le code de support est ici ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m»
idees.text_original: 2023: LLMs struggle with 4th grade word problems 2024: LLMs can do high school math 2025: LLMs get a gold medal at the IMO Now, GPT-5.6 solves famous frontier math/stat questions. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m
